title: Ptolemaic Egypt
subtitle: 332–30 BC · Alexander, the Greek Kingdom on the Nile, and the End with Cleopatra

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Alexander's conquest through the great Ptolemies and the long dynastic decline under Rome's shadow to Cleopatra VII

entries.label: Alexander the Great takes Egypt
entries.hint: Alexander entered Egypt in the winter of 332 to no resistance, the Persian satrap Mazaces handing it over. He sacrificed to the Apis bull at Memphis, was crowned there in pharaonic style, marked out the new city of Alexandria on the coast, and trekked to the oracle of Amun at Siwa, which is said to have greeted him as the god's son. He left within months, appointing Egyptian nomarchs under a Greek financial overseer, and never returned; his body did.
entries.note: Arrian, Anabasis 3.1–5; Diodorus 17.49–52; Curtius 4.7–8. Alexandria's foundation: P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972) vol.1 pp.3–7. Stanley Burstein, 'Alexander in Egypt', in Bosworth & Baynham (eds.), Alexander the Great in Fact and Fiction (2000).

entries.label: Philip Arrhidaeus and Alexander IV — the empty kingship
entries.hint: After Alexander's death Egypt was ruled in the name of his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his posthumous son Alexander IV, but governed by the satrap Ptolemy, who intercepted Alexander's funeral cortège and installed the body at Memphis (later Alexandria) as a talisman of legitimacy. Both Argead kings were murdered in the succession wars — Arrhidaeus in 317, the boy Alexander IV around 309 — leaving Ptolemy free to take the crown himself.
entries.note: Diodorus 18.3, 18.28 (the funeral carriage), 19.105 (Alexander IV's death). Pausanias 1.6.3. Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001) pp.14–20.

entries.label: Ptolemy I Soter — the founder
entries.hint: Ptolemy son of Lagos, one of Alexander's marshals, turned the satrapy of Egypt into a hereditary Greek kingdom. He beat off Perdiccas's invasion in 321, fought the other Successors across Cyprus, Syria and the Aegean, and took the royal title in 305. He founded the state cult of Serapis, began the Museum and Library, wrote a sober history of Alexander's campaigns, and set the pattern the dynasty followed for three centuries — a Macedonian court at Alexandria over a bureaucratised Egyptian country.
entries.note: Satrap Stela (Cairo CG 22182), 311 BC. Diodorus 18–20; Ptolemy's lost history underlies Arrian. Hölbl (2001) pp.21–35; Walter Ellis, Ptolemy of Egypt (1994).

entries.label: Ptolemy II Philadelphus — the golden age
entries.hint: Under Ptolemy II the Museum and Library reached their height, the Pharos lighthouse was finished, and a spectacular procession through Alexandria advertised the dynasty's wealth to the Greek world. He married his full sister Arsinoe II, and the pair were worshipped as the 'Sibling Gods'. He re-cut the Nile–Red Sea canal, planted Greek soldier-settlers across a newly drained Faiyum, financed the Alexandrian poets, and fought the first two of the long Syrian Wars.
entries.note: Grand Procession: Kallixeinos of Rhodes via Athenaeus 5.196–203; E.E. Rice, The Grand Procession of Ptolemy Philadelphus (1983). Faiyum: the Zenon archive. Hölbl (2001) pp.35–46, 61–63.

entries.label: Ptolemy III Euergetes — the empire at its widest
entries.hint: In the Third Syrian War Ptolemy III marched east as far as Babylon and beyond, according to his own Adulis inscription, and brought home cult statues the Persians had carried off from Egypt centuries before — earning the title Euergetes, 'Benefactor'. His empire reached its greatest extent, taking in coastal strips from Thrace to Cyrenaica. He began the great temple of Horus at Edfu in 237 and issued the Canopus Decree, a priestly synod's attempt to fix the drifting calendar with a leap day.
entries.note: Adulis inscription: OGIS 54; Cosmas Indicopleustes preserves it. Canopus Decree (Cairo CG 22186 and the Tanis and Kom el-Hisn copies), 238 BC. Edfu foundation: the temple's own building texts. Hölbl (2001) pp.46–52.

entries.label: Ptolemy IV Philopator — Raphia and the turn
entries.hint: Ptolemy IV won the Fourth Syrian War at Raphia in 217, but only by arming and training some 20,000 native Egyptians as a phalanx — a decision Polybius blamed for the revolts that followed, since the men who had won the battle would not go back to being subjects. His court was run by the ministers Sosibius and Agathocles, who had his mother and brother killed; the king is drawn in the sources as an indolent aesthete, and his death in 204 was concealed while the ministers seized power.
entries.note: Polybius 5.34–87 (Raphia and its consequences). Raphia Decree (trilingual; Cairo and Pithom copies), 217 BC. The palace coup on his death: Polybius 15.25–33. Hölbl (2001) pp.127–33.

entries.label: Ptolemy V Epiphanes — the Rosetta king
entries.hint: Ptolemy V came to the throne as a small child amid palace murders, a Delta revolt, and the ongoing secession of the Thebaid. Antiochus III seized Coele-Syria at the Battle of Panium in 200, and Rome stepped in as the boy-king's protector. His formal coronation at Memphis in 196 was marked by a priestly decree of thanks, cut in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek on the stone found at Rosetta in 1799 that unlocked the Egyptian scripts.
entries.note: Rosetta Stone / Memphis Decree (BM EA 24), 196 BC. Polybius 18.53–54; Livy 33.19–20. Hölbl (2001) pp.134–43, 153–59; Richard Parkinson, The Rosetta Stone (2005).

entries.label: Ptolemy VI Philometor — the reign of civil war and Rome
entries.hint: Ptolemy VI spent his reign at odds with his brother Ptolemy VIII, the two dividing and re-dividing the kingdom. When Antiochus IV invaded in 170 and 168 and stood outside Alexandria, only a Roman ultimatum — the envoy Popillius Laenas drawing a line in the sand — made him withdraw. Cyrenaica was split off for Ptolemy VIII by Roman arrangement. Philometor was, by the standards of the late dynasty, a capable king; he died of a fall from his horse campaigning in Syria.
entries.note: Polybius 28–29; Diodorus 31.1–2. The partition of the kingdom and Cyrene: the 'Testament of Ptolemy VIII' (SEG 9.7). Hölbl (2001) pp.143–52, 181–94.

entries.label: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II 'Physcon'
entries.hint: Ptolemy VIII returned from Cyrene on his brother's death to rule Egypt, marrying first his sister Cleopatra II and then, alongside her, his niece Cleopatra III. His war with Cleopatra II from 132 tore the country apart for a decade, ending in the amnesty decrees of 118. His purges of the Alexandrian Greek elite, remembered by Menecles of Barca, scattered scholars and artists across the Mediterranean and are often said to have ended Alexandria's cultural pre-eminence.
entries.note: The 118 BC amnesty decrees: P. Tebtunis I 5. Menecles of Barca on the intellectual exodus: FGrH 270 F 9 via Athenaeus 4.184b–c. Hölbl (2001) pp.194–203.

entries.label: The later Ptolemies — dynasty at war with itself
entries.hint: After Physcon the dynasty consumed itself in wars between Cleopatra III and her sons Ptolemy IX and Ptolemy X, and between the brothers. A revolt in the Thebaid was crushed in 88 with the sacking of Thebes, which never recovered. Rome inherited Cyrenaica in 96 and increasingly treated Egypt as a bequest waiting to be collected, its intervention held off only by the value of the grain and the size of the bribes.
entries.note: Pausanias 1.9; Justin 39. The 88 BC Theban revolt and sack: Pausanias 1.9.3. The 'will' bequeathing Egypt to Rome (Ptolemy X or XI): Cicero, De Rege Alexandrino. Hölbl (2001) pp.204–13.

entries.label: Ptolemy XII Auletes — the client king
entries.hint: Ptolemy XII bought Roman recognition of his rule in 59 BC with a bribe to Caesar and Pompey said to be 6,000 talents, borrowed from the financier Rabirius. He could not prevent Rome annexing Cyprus in 58, was driven out by an Alexandrian mob, and was put back on his throne in 55 by the Syrian governor Gabinius, who left a garrison of Roman soldiers behind. He died in 51 having pledged Egypt's revenues to his Roman creditors and named his daughter Cleopatra and a son as joint heirs.
entries.note: Cicero, letters and Pro Rabirio Postumo; Dio Cassius 39.12–16, 39.55–58. Hölbl (2001) pp.222–30; Mary Siani-Davies, 'Ptolemy XII Auletes and the Romans', Historia 46 (1997).

entries.label: Cleopatra VII Philopator
entries.hint: Cleopatra VII ruled first with her brother Ptolemy XIII, who drove her out; Julius Caesar, arriving in 48, restored her, fought the Alexandrian War for her, and fathered her son Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she backed and then married Mark Antony, bore him three children, and received from him at the Donations of Alexandria in 34 grants of Roman eastern territory for her children. Octavian's propaganda made her Rome's enemy; defeat at Actium in 31 and his invasion in 30 ended the dynasty, and she took her own life.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony; Dio Cassius 42–51; Caesar, Bellum Alexandrinum. Duane Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010); Joyce Tyldesley, Cleopatra: Last Queen of Egypt (2008).

entries.label: Caesarion — the last king
entries.hint: Ptolemy XV Caesar, called Caesarion, was Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar and her co-ruler from the age of three, styled 'King of Kings' at the Donations of Alexandria. After Actium his mother sent him toward the Red Sea and India for safety, but he was lured back and killed on Octavian's orders — reportedly on the advice 'it is not good to have too many Caesars'. With him the three-thousand-year line of Egyptian kingship ended.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony 81–82; Suetonius, Augustus 17; Dio Cassius 51.15. The 'too many Caesars' line attributed to the philosopher Arius via Plutarch.

entries.group: The Native Pharaohs of the Thebaid
entries.label: Horwennefer and Ankhwennefer — the rebel kings of Thebes
entries.hint: During the Great Revolt of the Thebaid, Upper Egypt seceded under two successive native kings, Horwennefer and then Ankhwennefer, who took full pharaonic titles, dated documents by their own regnal years, were recognised by the Theban temples, and drew support from the Kingdom of Meroe to the south. They held Thebes and much of the south for the better part of twenty years before a Ptolemaic army under Komanos defeated Ankhwennefer in 186; an amnesty decree formally closed the war.
entries.note: Demotic and Greek documents dated by their reigns; the Philae priestly decree of 186 recording the victory. Anne-Emmanuelle Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes': Recherches sur les troubles intérieurs en Égypte du règne de Ptolémée III à la conquête romaine (2004); Hölbl (2001) pp.153–59.

entries.group: The Native Pharaohs of the Thebaid
entries.label: Harsiese — a native king in the dynastic war
entries.hint: While Ptolemy VIII and Cleopatra II fought their civil war, a man named Harsiese was briefly proclaimed king at Thebes, issuing at least one order to a bank and appearing in a handful of Demotic documents before vanishing from the record. His short-lived kingship shows that native royal claims in the south could still resurface whenever the dynasty's grip slipped.
entries.note: P. Amherst 51 and related Demotic texts; Pieter Pestman, 'Haronnophris and Chaonnophris', in Vleeming (ed.), Hundred-Gated Thebes (1995); Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes' (2004).

entries.label: The ruling Cleopatras
entries.hint: Long before Cleopatra VII, the dynasty gave real power to its queens. Cleopatra I, a Seleucid princess, ruled as regent for her son Ptolemy V and issued coinage and decrees in her own name. Cleopatra II was co-ruler, then led an armed revolt against her brother-husband Ptolemy VIII and held Alexandria for years. Cleopatra III wielded decisive influence over her sons' reigns. The pattern of the queen as an independent centre of power was a Ptolemaic institution.
entries.note: Cleopatra I's regency: Polybius 22.3; coins and dating formulae. Cleopatra II's revolt: the 132–124 BC documents. Grace Macurdy, Hellenistic Queens (1932); Elizabeth Carney, Arsinoë of Egypt and Macedon (2013) for the wider pattern.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars of the Successors, the Syrian Wars, Raphia and the native phalanx, the Great Revolt of the Thebaid, and Actium

entries.label: Alexander takes Egypt
entries.hint: Alexander's army crossed Sinai and reached Pelusium in the autumn of 332; the Persian satrap Mazaces, left without troops after Issus and the fall of the Levant, surrendered the country. There was no battle. Alexander sailed up the Nile to Memphis, was received as a liberator from Persian rule, held games and sacrifices, and turned the moment into a change of dynasty rather than a conquest.
entries.note: Arrian, Anabasis 3.1; Curtius 4.7.1–5. Stanley Burstein, 'Alexander in Egypt: Continuity or Change?', in Achaemenid History 8 (1994).

entries.label: Ptolemy secures Egypt
entries.hint: Ptolemy fought off the other marshals to keep Egypt. In 321 the regent Perdiccas invaded and lost thousands of men trying to force the Nile at Memphis, drowned or taken by crocodiles, and was killed by his own officers. Ptolemy then contested Cyprus, Cyrene and Coele-Syria for two decades, winning the Battle of Gaza in 312 and losing ground again, until the coalition victory over Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 left him securely holding Egypt and southern Syria.
entries.note: Diodorus 18.33–36 (Perdiccas at the Nile), 19.80–86 (Gaza), 20.113, 21.1 (Ipsus). Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001) pp.14–24; Richard Billows, Antigonos the One-Eyed (1990).

entries.label: The Syrian Wars
entries.hint: For over a century the Ptolemies and the Seleucids fought six wars, chiefly over Coele-Syria — the southern Levant, its ports, timber and taxes. Ptolemaic power crested in the Third War, when Ptolemy III overran Seleucid territory to the Euphrates; it broke in the Fifth, when Antiochus III took the province for good. The wars drained both kingdoms and drew in Rome, which ended the last of them with the ultimatum of 168.
entries.note: Polybius 5, 15, 28–29; the Gurob Papyrus (Third War). Overview: John Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010); Hölbl (2001) pp.38–52, 134–43.

entries.label: The Battle of Raphia
entries.hint: At Raphia on the Gaza coast Ptolemy IV met Antiochus III with about 70,000 men and 73 African elephants against 68,000 and 102 Indian elephants. Antiochus' elephants and right wing broke through, but Ptolemy's centre — including 20,000 Egyptians newly trained in the Macedonian phalanx — held and won the day. Egypt kept Coele-Syria for another seventeen years, and a trilingual decree celebrated the victory; but the armed and confident native soldiery was a new political fact.
entries.note: Polybius 5.79–87. Raphia Decree, 217 BC (Pithom and Memphis copies). Bezalel Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976) pp.128–41.

entries.label: The Great Revolt of the Thebaid
entries.hint: Beginning in the confusion after Ptolemy IV's death, Upper Egypt seceded under native pharaohs at Thebes and stayed out of Ptolemaic control for twenty years, funded partly by the temples and aided from Meroe. A separate rising in the Delta was crushed by Ptolemy V at Lycopolis, and the amnesty of 197 brought a brief peace. The Thebaid was only reconquered in 186; the temples of the south paid for their support with new controls and levies.
entries.note: Polybius 22.17; the Rosetta and Philae decrees. Anne-Emmanuelle Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes' (2004); Brian McGing, 'Revolt Egyptian Style', Archiv für Papyrusforschung 43 (1997).

entries.label: The Battle of Panium and the loss of the empire
entries.hint: At Panium, near the sources of the Jordan, Antiochus III destroyed the Ptolemaic field army under Scopas. Coele-Syria, held since Ptolemy I, passed permanently to the Seleucids. It was the effective end of the Ptolemaic overseas empire: within a generation Cyprus and Cyrene were all that remained abroad, and the kingdom shrank back to the Nile valley, dependent on Rome to guarantee even that.
entries.note: Polybius 16.18–19, 28.1; the 'Battle of Panium' fragment. Hölbl (2001) pp.134–39; Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010) pp.245–58.

entries.label: The Day of Eleusis
entries.hint: Antiochus IV, master of Egypt after two invasions and camped in the suburbs of Alexandria, was met by the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas carrying the Senate's decree that he leave Egypt. When Antiochus asked for time to consult his advisers, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around him with his staff and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus withdrew. Rome had settled the fate of the Hellenistic east without fighting.
entries.note: Polybius 29.27; Livy 45.12; Diodorus 31.2. The episode's date is 30 June 168 BC (a lunar eclipse fixes it). Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984).

entries.label: The dynasty at war with itself
entries.hint: From Ptolemy VI on, the Ptolemies fought each other more than any foreign enemy: brother against brother, mother against son, the mob of Alexandria against whichever king it disliked, the chora against the capital. Cleopatra II held Alexandria in arms against Ptolemy VIII for a decade; a Theban revolt was put down in 88 with the sacking of the ancient city. Each round of civil war spent revenue, wrecked administration, and made Roman arbitration harder to refuse.
entries.note: Polybius 31, 39; Diodorus 33–34; Justin 38–39. The sack of Thebes: Pausanias 1.9.3. Hölbl (2001) pp.181–213.

entries.label: Actium and the annexation of Egypt
entries.hint: Antony and Cleopatra's fleet was beaten off Actium in western Greece in September 31, and their forces melted away over the following year. Octavian invaded Egypt from Syria in the summer of 30, took Pelusium and then Alexandria; Antony and then Cleopatra killed themselves, and Caesarion was hunted down and executed. Octavian annexed Egypt as his personal possession, governed by a prefect of equestrian rank and closed to senators — the wealthiest single addition ever made to the Roman state.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony 60–86; Dio Cassius 50–51; Suetonius, Augustus 17. The settlement: P.A. Brunt & J.M. Moore, Res Gestae Divi Augusti (1967); Alan Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.37–44.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A Greek kingdom over an Egyptian country — the dioiketes, the cleruchy, bilingual bureaucracy, and the priestly synods

entries.label: A Greek kingdom over an Egyptian country
entries.hint: The Ptolemaic state ran on a double footing. A Macedonian-Greek ruling class governed from Alexandria, and three Greek cities — Alexandria, Ptolemais in the south, and old Naukratis — kept Greek civic institutions. The rest of the country, the chora, was administered by adapted pharaonic methods in Greek and Demotic. Greek and Egyptian law both had force; the king was basileus to the Greeks and Pharaoh to the Egyptians, and largely kept the two worlds in separate documents.
entries.note: Naphtali Lewis, Greeks in Ptolemaic Egypt (1986); Alan K. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.21–36. The legal duality: Joseph Mélèze Modrzejewski, 'Law and Justice in Ptolemaic Egypt', in Geller & Maehler (eds.), Legal Documents of the Hellenistic World (1995).

entries.label: The dioiketes and the fiscal machine
entries.hint: Ptolemy II built the most systematically extractive government the ancient world had seen, run by a chief finance minister, the dioiketes. Every nome had a royal scribe keeping a fresh land-and-crop survey, an economic officer, and a military governor; taxes on land, orchards, salt, beer, oil and dozens of trades were farmed out to bidders backed by sureties; and a set of Revenue Laws laid down the procedure. The minister Apollonios and his agent Zenon left an archive of over 1,700 documents showing it at work.
entries.note: Revenue Laws Papyrus (P. Rev.), 259 BC: Bingen, Le papyrus Revenue Laws (1952). Zenon archive: Pieter Pestman, A Guide to the Zenon Archive (1981). Sitta von Reden, Money in Ptolemaic Egypt (2007).

entries.label: The cleruchy
entries.hint: The Ptolemies settled their soldiers on the land. A cleruch received a plot of royal ground — larger for cavalry, smaller for infantry — held rent-light in return for turning out when summoned, and increasingly passed to his sons. The policy planted tens of thousands of Greek, Thracian, Jewish and other military families across the countryside, above all in the reclaimed Faiyum, creating a Hellenised rural elite alongside the Egyptian peasantry and, at Raphia, extending to armed Egyptians too.
entries.note: Jane Rowlandson (ed.), Women and Society in Greek and Roman Egypt (1998) on cleruchic families; Christelle Fischer-Bovet, Army and Society in Ptolemaic Egypt (2014). The Faiyum toponymy (Philadelphia, Theadelphia, etc.) records the settlement.

entries.label: The bilingual archive
entries.hint: Ptolemaic government generated paper on an unprecedented scale, and Egypt's dry sand kept it. Greek was the language of the higher administration; Demotic served private Egyptian law and the temples; official notaries of both kinds registered contracts. The surviving papyri — the Zenon, Tebtunis, Herakleopolis and other archives, and later the vast Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds — make Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt the best-documented pre-modern society anywhere.
entries.note: Roger Bagnall, Reading Papyri, Writing Ancient History (1995); E.G. Turner, Greek Papyri: An Introduction (1968). Tebtunis: Grenfell, Hunt & Smyly, The Tebtunis Papyri (1902– ).

entries.label: The priestly synods and the trilingual decrees
entries.hint: The high priests of Egypt's temples met in assembly, at first yearly, to conduct business with the crown: confirming honours for the king, setting festival calendars, and negotiating the temples' privileges and obligations. Their honorific decrees — issued at Canopus in 238, at Memphis for Ptolemy IV in 217 and for Ptolemy V in 196 — were published in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and are the formal record of the bargain between the Greek monarchy and the Egyptian religious establishment.
entries.note: Canopus Decree (Cairo CG 22186); Raphia Decree; Memphis Decree / Rosetta Stone (BM EA 24). Stefan Pfeiffer, Das Dekret von Kanopos (2004); Christophe Thiers on the synodal decree corpus.

entries.label: Greek courts, Egyptian courts, and the petition
entries.hint: Justice ran on parallel tracks: royal circuit judges (chrematistai) applied Greek law, Egyptian judges (laokritai) applied Egyptian law, and litigants could sometimes choose. Above both, any subject could send a written petition (enteuxis) to the king — in practice to an official acting in his name — and thousands survive, from stolen donkeys to violent assault to fraud by a tax-farmer. A decree of 118 BC set rules for which court heard cases between Greeks and Egyptians.
entries.note: P. Tebtunis I 5 (the 118 BC decree). Petitions: John Bauschatz, Law and Enforcement in Ptolemaic Egypt (2013); the enteuxeis of P. Enteuxeis (O. Guéraud, 1931). Modrzejewski, The Laws of Moses and the Laws of Egypt.

entries.label: Rome the overlord
entries.hint: Rome's grip tightened by stages. From 200 it was the boy Ptolemy V's protector; in 168 its envoy turned Antiochus IV out of Egypt with a word; in 59 Ptolemy XII bought recognition of his throne with a colossal bribe raised from Roman lenders; in 55 a Roman army restored him and left a garrison. By the time Cleopatra VII took the throne the kingdom's revenues were pledged to Roman financiers and its independence was a formality Rome could revoke at will.
entries.note: Polybius; Cicero, Pro Rabirio Postumo and letters. Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984) vol.2; Mary Siani-Davies, Cicero's Speech Pro Rabirio Postumo (2001).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Serapis and the dynastic cult, the Egyptian temple rebuilt at its grandest, and the meeting of Greek and Egyptian gods

entries.label: Serapis and the cult of the living king
entries.hint: Ptolemy I promoted Serapis — the Memphite Osiris-Apis reshaped with a Greek-god's face and body — as a deity both Greeks and Egyptians could worship, and built him a great temple on the Alexandrian acropolis. The dynasty also had itself worshipped: living Ptolemies and their queens received divine cult, an eponymous priest of Alexander and the deified rulers headed the state calendar, and Arsinoe II after her death was given her own priestess and a share in every temple in the land.
entries.note: John E. Stambaugh, Sarapis under the Early Ptolemies (1972). Ruler cult: Ludwig Koenen, 'The Ptolemaic King as a Religious Figure', in Bulloch et al. (eds.), Images and Ideologies (1993). Arsinoe: the Mendes Stela; Elizabeth Carney, Arsinoë of Egypt and Macedon (2013).

entries.label: The Egyptian temple rebuilt at its grandest
entries.hint: The Ptolemies, for all their Greekness, poured resources into Egyptian temples, and the best-preserved of all Egyptian temples are theirs. The temple of Horus at Edfu, begun in 237 and finished 180 years later, stands almost complete, its walls a library of ritual, myth and temple lore in dense Ptolemaic hieroglyphs. Dendera, Kom Ombo, Esna, Philae and the birth-houses belong to the same programme — the classic Egyptian sanctuary in its final, most elaborate form.
entries.note: Dieter Arnold, Temples of the Last Pharaohs (1999) pp.137–224. Edfu texts: the Chassinat/Rochemonteix edition, Le temple d'Edfou (1892– ); Sylvie Cauville's studies. Philae: the pre-flood documentation.

entries.label: The meeting of Greek and Egyptian gods
entries.hint: Three centuries of coexistence blended the two religious worlds. Isis grew from an Egyptian goddess into a Mediterranean-wide saviour, her powers catalogued in Greek 'aretalogies' that begin 'I am Isis'; Thoth was read as Hermes Trismegistos; the child Horus became Harpocrates. Greeks in Egypt worshipped Egyptian gods under Greek names and Egyptian priests wrote their theology in Greek forms, while the temples of the chora carried on in pure Egyptian idiom.
entries.note: Isis aretalogies: the Kyme, Maroneia and Andros texts; Jan Bergman, Ich bin Isis (1968). Françoise Dunand, Le culte d'Isis dans le bassin oriental de la Méditerranée (1973). David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998) for the later trajectory.

entries.label: The animal cults under royal patronage
entries.hint: The Ptolemies funded and joined Egypt's animal cults. Kings attended the enthronement and burial of the Apis at Memphis and the Buchis bull at Armant, whose gallery cemetery, the Bucheum, and the associated Mothers-of-Buchis cemetery date largely to this period. The ibis, falcon, cat and crocodile necropoleis stayed busy, and the votive-mummy industry — a prayer carried to a god by a purpose-mummified animal — reached its greatest scale.
entries.note: Robert Mond & Oliver Myers, The Bucheum, 3 vols. (1934). Dorothy Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (1988, 2nd ed. 2012) on the Apis. Salima Ikram (ed.), Divine Creatures (2005).

entries.label: The Jews of Egypt and the temple of Onias
entries.hint: Egypt held the largest Jewish community outside Judaea — two of Alexandria's five districts, and settlements across the chora, many descended from soldiers. Their synagogues (proseuchai) carried dedications 'on behalf of King Ptolemy'. Around 160 BC the exiled Zadokite high priest Onias IV was allowed to build a functioning Jewish temple at Leontopolis, which operated for over two centuries — the tradition within which the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, the Septuagint, took shape.
entries.note: Josephus, Antiquities 12–13, Jewish War 7.10.2–4 (Onias' temple); the Letter of Aristeas (Septuagint legend). Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum (Tcherikover & Fuks, 1957–64); Sylvie Honigman, The Septuagint and Homeric Scholarship in Alexandria (2003).

entries.label: The Oracle of the Potter and apocalyptic
entries.hint: A strand of Demotic literature turned religion against the Greeks. The Oracle of the Potter, surviving in Greek translations from Egyptian, prophesies that the 'city by the sea' — Alexandria — will be emptied and become a place where fishermen dry their nets, its founding god departing to Memphis, and that a saviour king 'sent by the Sun' will restore Egypt and its temples. The Demotic Chronicle reads the succession of kings for the same promise of deliverance from foreign rule.
entries.note: Oracle of the Potter: Ludwig Koenen, Die Prophezeiungen des Toepfers, ZPE 2 (1968) and later. Demotic Chronicle: P. BN 215. David Frankfurter, Elijah in Upper Egypt (1993) pp.159–94 on the apocalyptic tradition.
